title: Phases, Seasons and Time Zones
description: How lunar phases cycle, why sidereal and synodic months differ, the cause of seasons.
content_html:
The Lunar Phase Cycle

The Moon does not produce its own light. The phases we see are simply different proportions of the Moon’s sunlit hemisphere facing Earth as the Moon orbits us. To understand phases, imagine looking down on the Earth–Moon system from above the North Pole: the Moon orbits anticlockwise, and the Sun illuminates half the Moon at any time. As the Moon’s position changes relative to Earth and Sun, we see different fractions of that illuminated half.

The eight named phases, in order, are:

  • New Moon — Moon is between Earth and Sun; the near side faces away from sunlight; the Moon is not visible.
  • Waxing Crescent — a thin sliver of lit surface becomes visible in the west after sunset.
  • First Quarter — the Moon is 90° east of the Sun; the right half of the near side is lit; rises around midday and sets around midnight.
  • Waxing Gibbous — more than half the near side is lit, still growing (‘waxing’).
  • Full Moon — Earth is between Moon and Sun; the entire near side is lit; rises at sunset, sets at sunrise.
  • Waning Gibbous — the lit fraction is decreasing (‘waning’).
  • Last Quarter — the left half of the near side is lit; rises around midnight and sets around midday.
  • Waning Crescent — a thin sliver visible in the east before sunrise; completes the cycle back to new moon.
Key Fact

Eight phase names in order: New Moon, Waxing Crescent, First Quarter, Waxing Gibbous, Full Moon, Waning Gibbous, Last Quarter, Waning Crescent. ‘Waxing’ means growing; ‘waning’ means shrinking.

Sidereal Month vs Synodic Month

Just as there are two types of day, there are two types of month. The sidereal month is the time for the Moon to orbit Earth relative to the distant stars: approximately 27.3 days. However, because Earth is simultaneously moving around the Sun, the Moon must travel a little further along its orbit to re-align with the Sun and return to the same phase. This longer period — 29.5 days — is the synodic month, sometimes called the lunar month. It is the synodic month that governs the visible phase cycle and is used for lunar calendars.

The difference between 27.3 and 29.5 days arises for exactly the same geometrical reason as the difference between a sidereal and solar day: Earth’s orbital motion means the Moon must ‘catch up’ an additional ~27° of arc before the Sun, Earth and Moon return to the same relative geometry.

A common exam mistake is to mix up 27.3 and 29.5 days. A reliable memory hook: 27.3 is the shorter period (relative to the ‘fixed’ stars) and is the Moon’s true orbital period. 29.5 is the longer period (relative to the Sun) and is what drives the phase cycle a human observer notices. If asked which period ‘controls the phase cycle’, answer synodic (29.5 days). If asked for the Moon’s orbital period or the sidereal month, answer 27.3 days.

Seasons: Axial Tilt, Not Distance

One of the most persistent misconceptions in science education is that seasons are caused by Earth getting closer to or further from the Sun. This is wrong for a simple reason: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January (perihelion, ~147 million km) — which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere. Distance to the Sun plays almost no role in seasons.

Seasons are caused by Earth’s axial tilt of 23.5°. Because the axis always points in the same direction in space (toward Polaris), different hemispheres are tilted toward or away from the Sun at different times of year:

  • At the June solstice (around 21 June), the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun. Sunlight arrives at a steeper angle, is more concentrated per unit area, and the days are longer — producing summer in the North.
  • At the December solstice (around 21 December), the Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun. The Northern Hemisphere has longer nights and shallower, more spread-out sunlight — producing winter.
  • At the two equinoxes (March and September), neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, and day and night are of roughly equal length worldwide.

The variation in sunrise and sunset time throughout the year follows directly from the axial tilt: at the summer solstice in the UK, the Sun rises as early as about 04:45 BST (in June), while at the winter solstice it may not rise until after 08:00 GMT. Observers at or above the Arctic Circle (66.5° N) experience the midnight Sun around the June solstice — 24 hours of daylight.

Key Fact

Seasons are caused by Earth’s 23.5° axial tilt, not by changes in Earth–Sun distance. The tilt causes two seasonal effects: (1) the angle of incoming sunlight (steeper in summer = more concentrated); (2) the length of daylight hours (longer in summer).

Time Zones and Greenwich Mean Time

If every location kept its own Local Mean Time, clocks would differ from one town to the next, making international travel and communication chaotic. The solution, adopted from the late nineteenth century, is to divide the world into time zones: bands roughly 15° of longitude wide (since Earth rotates 15° per hour), each sharing a standard clock time offset from Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) by a whole number of hours.

GMT is the Local Mean Time at the Prime Meridian (0° longitude, Greenwich). It serves as the international reference from which all other time zones are offset. Universal Time (UT) is a modern refinement of GMT that uses atomic clocks and is essentially identical to GMT for most astronomical purposes.

The relationship between longitude and time is precise: Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so it rotates 15° per hour or 1° per 4 minutes. A location 30° east of Greenwich is therefore 2 hours ahead of GMT; a location 75° west of Greenwich is 5 hours behind GMT. Time zones allow a location to keep clock noon near solar noon, within ±30 minutes for most standard zones.

Determining a ship’s longitude at sea was one of the greatest practical problems of the eighteenth century. Two methods competed. The lunar distance method used precise measurements of the angle between the Moon and a reference star to determine GMT from published tables, then compared it with local solar time to calculate longitude. This required skilled calculation but no accurate portable clock. The horological method, championed by clockmaker John Harrison, used a highly accurate marine chronometer that kept GMT regardless of conditions at sea. By reading local apparent solar noon from a sextant and comparing it with the chronometer’s GMT reading, a navigator could calculate longitude directly. Harrison’s chronometer (the H4, completed in 1759) ultimately solved the problem and won much of the Board of Longitude prize. Both methods required understanding the relationship between time and longitude (4 min per degree).
exam_tip_html: For lunar phase questions, always describe both the Moon’s position relative to Earth and Sun AND its appearance from Earth — saying ‘new moon’ is not enough without explaining that the near side faces away from the Sun. For seasons, never say distance to the Sun causes seasons — this costs marks. The two effects of axial tilt are: angle of incidence of sunlight (steeper = more energy per unit area) and day length (longer summer days mean more total energy received). For time zone calculations, remember 15° = 1 hour and 1° = 4 minutes — write this as a formula, then substitute numbers clearly. Always state whether the location is east (ahead of GMT) or west (behind GMT).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The eight named lunar phases run new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent, completing a synodic month of 29.5 days. The sidereal month (true orbital period relative to the stars) is 27.3 days.
  • Seasons are caused by Earth’s 23.5° axial tilt, which changes the angle and duration of incoming sunlight at each latitude — not by changes in Earth–Sun distance.
  • Time zones are 15°-wide longitude bands offset from GMT in whole hours. GMT is Local Mean Time at the Prime Meridian (Greenwich); Universal Time (UT) is its modern atomic-clock equivalent.

practice_questions.text:
Which phase of the Moon occurs when it is positioned between Earth and the Sun?
A) Full Moon
B) First Quarter
C) New Moon
D) Last Quarter
State the duration of a synodic month.
State the two effects of Earth's axial tilt that combine to produce hotter summers in the Northern Hemisphere.
practice_questions.marks: Sunlight arrives at a steeper angle in summer, concentrating more energy per unit area of ground [1]; days are longer in summer, so Earth receives more hours of solar heating [1].

practice_questions.text: A city is located at longitude 45° East. Calculate the difference between its local clock time and Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), and state whether it is ahead of or behind GMT.
practice_questions.marks: 15° = 1 hour; 45° East = 45 / 15 = 3 hours ahead of GMT [1]; the city is 3 hours ahead of GMT (GMT + 3) [1].

practice_questions.text: Dr Halima Yousef is explaining the difference between the sidereal month and the synodic month to a group of secondary students at her planetarium. Compare the two periods, state their durations, and explain why the synodic month is longer than the sidereal month.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sidereal month: time for Moon to complete one orbit relative to the distant stars; 27.3 days [1]. Synodic month: time for Moon to complete one phase cycle (e.g. new moon to new moon) relative to the Sun; 29.5 days [1]. The synodic month is longer because, during the 27.3 days of one orbit, Earth has itself moved along its orbit around the Sun [1]; the Moon must therefore travel an additional ~27° of arc to re-align with the Earth-Sun direction and return to the same phase [1].
Secure: Three of four marking points.
Developing: States the two durations but cannot explain why the synodic month is longer.
Emerging: One duration stated only.

practice_questions.text:
The Brackenfell Observing Society is planning observations for the coming month. They want to observe: (a) the waxing gibbous moon, (b) the midnight sun phenomenon from Scandinavia in June, and (c) the exact moment of the March equinox.

For each of the three observations, explain the astronomical cause of the phenomenon and describe what the observer would see. Your answer should demonstrate understanding of lunar phases, the effects of axial tilt, and the geometry of the Earth-Sun system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6):
(a) Waxing gibbous: occurs when the Moon is between first quarter and full moon — more than half the near side is lit, with the lit fraction increasing ('waxing'); the Moon rises in the afternoon and is high in the sky by late evening [1]; it is caused by the Moon's position being roughly 90° to 180° east of the Sun, so the portion of the sunlit hemisphere visible from Earth is greater than half [1].
(b) Midnight Sun: above the Arctic Circle (66.5° N) around the June solstice, the Sun does not set for 24 hours; the observer sees the Sun skimming the northern horizon at midnight without dipping below it [1]; caused by Earth's 23.5° axial tilt meaning the North Pole is tilted toward the Sun — the Arctic Circle and beyond receive continuous sunlight during this period [1].
(c) March equinox: the Sun rises due east and sets due west; day and night are approximately equal in length worldwide; the Sun crosses the celestial equator moving northward [1]; caused by Earth's orbital position such that neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun — the axial tilt is side-on relative to the Earth-Sun direction [1].
Secure (3-4): Two of three phenomena explained with cause and observation.
Developing (1-2): One phenomenon explained adequately.
Emerging (0): No credit-worthy content.

flashcard_questions.q: List all eight lunar phases in order starting from new moon.
flashcard_questions.a: New Moon, Waxing Crescent, First Quarter, Waxing Gibbous, Full Moon, Waning Gibbous, Last Quarter, Waning Crescent.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'waxing' mean in the context of the Moon's phase?
flashcard_questions.a: The lit fraction of the Moon's disc as seen from Earth is growing (increasing).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the synodic month and how long does it last?
flashcard_questions.a: The time from one new moon to the next — approximately 29.5 days.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the sidereal month and how long does it last?
flashcard_questions.a: The Moon's orbital period relative to the stars — approximately 27.3 days.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the synodic month longer than the sidereal month?
flashcard_questions.a: Earth moves along its orbit during the Moon's orbit, so the Moon must travel further to realign with the Sun and return to the same phase.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the real cause of Earth's seasons?
flashcard_questions.a: Earth's 23.5° axial tilt, which changes the angle of sunlight and the length of daylight at each latitude throughout the year.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does distance from the Sun NOT cause seasons?
flashcard_questions.a: Earth is actually closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January — during Northern Hemisphere winter — not summer.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the equinoxes and when do they occur?
flashcard_questions.a: The two moments (around 21 March and 23 September) when neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun and day equals night worldwide.
The local mean time at the Prime Meridian (0° longitude, Greenwich), used as the international reference for civil timekeeping.

flashcard_questions.q: How many degrees of longitude correspond to one hour of time difference?
flashcard_questions.a: 15° — because Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours (15° per hour, or 1° per 4 minutes).

flashcard_questions.q: What role did John Harrison's marine chronometer play in solving the longitude problem?
flashcard_questions.a: It kept accurate GMT at sea, allowing navigators to compare local solar noon with GMT to calculate their longitude (4 min = 1°).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the midnight Sun and where can it be observed?
flashcard_questions.a: The Sun remaining above the horizon for 24 hours; observed above the Arctic Circle around the June solstice (above the Antarctic Circle around the December solstice).

glossary_terms.definition: The phase when the Moon lies between Earth and Sun; the Moon's near side is unlit and not visible from Earth.
The time for the Moon to complete one orbit of Earth relative to the distant stars; approximately 27.3 days.
The time for the Moon to return to the same phase (e.g. new moon to new moon); approximately 29.5 days. Also called the lunar month.
The two moments each year (around 21 March and 23 September) when the Sun crosses the celestial equator and day and night are of approximately equal length worldwide.
The local mean time at the Prime Meridian (0° longitude, Greenwich, London), used as the international reference for civil timekeeping.
Either of the two moments in the year when the Sun reaches its maximum angular distance north or south of the celestial equator, giving the longest and shortest days.
A historical technique for determining longitude at sea by measuring the angle between the Moon and a reference star and comparing it with published tables to find Greenwich Mean Time.
The use of an accurate marine chronometer to keep Greenwich Mean Time at sea, allowing longitude to be calculated by comparing it with local apparent solar time.
